activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
David got on the school bus. It was his first day of school. He held his mama's hand, then let go. "Which seat is mine?" he asked. "Any seat that is empty," said the bus driver.

David found a seat next to a tall girl. She had a big pink bow. The tall girl smiled at him. The bus went beep, beep, and started to roll.

David looked out the window. He saw his house get small. He saw trees go by fast. Then he saw a dog. The dog ran after the bus. David laughed. "Why is the dog running?" he asked. "Because the bus is fast," said the tall girl. "The wheels go round and round. That makes the bus move. The dog wants to chase it."

David looked down at the wheels. They were big. They went round and round, just like she said. "Wow!" said David. "Wheels make the bus go!"

The tall girl had a phone in her bag. Her mama gave it to her. "My mama said the phone can call home," she said. "If I need help, I press the green button. She will teach me how after school."

The bus stopped at the school. The doors opened wide. David jumped down the steps. He saw a big red door. He saw kids running to the line. "This is school!" said David. He ran to the door as fast as the dog.

"Wait for me!" he called to the tall girl. She ran too, and her pink bow flapped like wings.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everett did not want to open his mouth. He sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The man in the white coat smiled. "First we look," he said. He held up a little picture. Everett used his eyes to see it. It was a red truck. Then Everett closed his eyes. He could not see the truck at all. "My eyes see," said Everett.

Next the man shook a small bell. Ding, ding. Everett used his ears to hear it. He covered his ears with his hands. The bell went quiet. When he let go, he heard it again. "My ears hear," said Everett. His mom clapped. "Good trying," she said.

The man held a little orange for Everett to smell. His nose sniffed. It smelled sweet. Then came a tiny taste of juice on a stick. Everett's tongue tasted it. "Orange!" he said. At last the man tapped Everett's knee. His leg jumped up all by itself. His skin felt the tap. Everett wanted a sticker for being brave. But first the man said, "Say ah." Everett climbed down from the chair, took a big breath, and opened his mouth wide. The wet popsicle stick went in, then out. "All done," said the man. He held out a shiny sticker. Everett stuck it on his hand. "My hand can hold it," he said.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Madelyn wanted her red cup. It was up on the big counter. She reached up high. The cup did not move. She reached again. Still no cup.

Mom was in the kitchen. Madelyn said, "Cup." Mom looked at her. Then Mom waited. Madelyn thought hard. She tried new words. "Cup, please." Mom smiled big. "Yes! You asked so nicely." Mom got the red cup down. Madelyn held it with two hands.

Next, Madelyn wanted juice. She said, "Juice, please." Mom poured it in. Madelyn took a drink. "Thank you, Mom," she said. Mom clapped her hands.

Outside, the dog began to bark. A butterfly was on the fence. The dog jumped and barked at it. Then the butterfly flew away. The dog lay down. Soon the dog was asleep. Madelyn said, "The dog barked, so the butterfly flew." Dad heard her. "Good thinking, Madelyn!" Then Madelyn waved at the fence and said, "Bye, butterfly. Please come back tomorrow."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mia ran into the baby store. "The baby is coming soon!" she said. It was windy outside. The door went bang behind her. Snow fell past the big window. Mia had an idea. She would pick a cup for the baby.

Mia found a shiny red cup. It had a duck on it. "The baby will love this!" she said. Mom shook her head. "Watch this," said Mom. She gave the cup to a doll baby. The cup was too big. It did not fit in the doll's tiny mouth. Milk went all over.

Mia looked and looked. Then she found little bottles. They were small like her hands. Mom put a bottle to the doll's lips. It fit just right. "Babies drink from bottles," said Mia. "Not big cups!" She put the red cup back. She hugged the little bottle all the way to the car.

"Baby sister can drink now," said Mia. She patted Mom's big, warm tummy. "See you soon!"

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Victoria had a cold. She had to stay in bed all day.

She wanted to play outside. But the sky was cloudy. Mom said, "Rest today. Then you can play."

Victoria drank water. One cup. Two cups. Three cups. She ate warm soup. She slept a long nap.

Her brother Ben came in. He brought her teddy bear. "I hope you feel better," he said.

Victoria drank more water. One cup. Two cups. Three cups. She slept again.

The next morning, her nose was dry. Her cough was small. "Mom! My nose stopped running!"

Mom smiled. "You drank lots of water. Water helped your body get strong."

Victoria looked out the window. The sky was blue now. She saw the big tree in the yard.

"Can I go out now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Wrap up warm."

Victoria ran to the tree. She touched its rough bark. "I was sick, tree. Now I am better!"

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Edouard sat in the music room at school. Miss Rosa played a song on her drum. Boom, boom, boom, slow and steady. "Now we clap!" she said.

Edouard clapped very fast. Clap-clap-clap-clap! But his claps did not match the drum. He got all mixed up. He stopped. "Why am I wrong?" he asked. "The drum goes slow," he said. "I clapped too fast. That is why." So he waited. He listened to the boom, boom, boom. Then he clapped slow, like the drum. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. It fit!

Next Miss Rosa sang a rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Edouard only knew half of it. His brother sang this one at home, but the song felt so long. Edouard tried. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," he sang. Then he forgot the rest. He tried again. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are." He did it! He laughed out loud.

Miss Rosa laughed too. "You did it, Edouard!" she said. Edouard clapped a slow clap for himself. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. "I can do the whole song," he said, "all by myself!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexander went to the baby store with Mom. Mom said a baby was coming soon. Alexander wanted to pick a cup for the baby. He saw a red cup and a blue cup. Which one would the baby like?

He picked a cup with two handles. "Why two handles?" he asked. Mom let him hold a bottle filled with water. It was slippery and almost fell. Alexander held it with two hands and it stayed. "Two hands hold better," he said. The cup had two handles because babies hold with two hands!

He spun around in a happy circle. "The baby can drink all by himself!" Mom laughed and put the cup in the cart. At home, Alexander set the cup by the small baby bed. "I will show you how it works," he whispered to the empty bed.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Ava sat at the art table. She had a big pile of paper shapes. She wanted to make a house. "I will take the square for the walls," said Ava. She put a small square on top. Then she put a red triangle on the very top. "A roof!" she said.

Now Ava wanted wheels. She found two circles. She put a circle on the edge of the table. It rolled away! It rolled under the chair. "My circle is lost," said Ava. Her tummy felt tight. Miss Rosa came close and sat down beside her. "It is right here," said Miss Rosa. She picked up the circle and gave it back.

Ava tried again. She put the circle down flat. It stayed. She turned it up on its side. It rolled again! Ava watched. Then she said, "It rolls because it is round." She put both circles down flat, nice and safe. They did not roll. They did not get lost.

Ava painted her house with a rectangle door. She got blue paint on her skin, so Miss Rosa helped her wash it off. Ava held up her picture. The wheels were two big circles, sitting still. "Look at my house!" said Ava.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Madison ran onto the basketball court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak on the floor. Today was her first game with her team.

Madison wanted to score a basket. She threw the ball up high. It hit the rim and fell down. She tried again. It bounced off the side. Madison sat down on the dry, warm floor.

"Why does the ball not go in?" she asked her coach.

"Think about where your feet are," said Coach Kim, kindly.

Madison looked down. She stood very close to Coach Kim. Then she saw her spot on the floor. It had a small star sticker on it. She had not been standing on her star! She moved back and put both feet on the sticker. She threw the ball again. It went swish, right into the net.

"My feet were too close," said Madison. "The star is my spot."

Coach Kim smiled and clapped. "Good noticing, Madison."

The weather outside was sunny through the big window. Madison bounced the ball and giggled. "Can I try from my star again?" she asked.

"Yes," said Coach Kim. "You sure can."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Josephine's class had a bird nest up on a shelf. Miss Penny put five little eggs inside it. "Let's count the eggs," said Miss Penny. Everyone sang, "One, two, three, four, five."

Then it was snack time. Josephine wanted to pour juice into cups. Miss Penny put out ten cups in a long line. "Can you pour a little juice in each one?" she asked. Josephine felt worried. Ten was a lot. "What if I miss a cup?" she asked. Miss Penny smiled. "Just count as you pour."

Josephine poured. "One, two, three, five," she said. A boy named Max looked grumpy. "You missed a cup!" he said. It was still empty. Josephine looked at it. "I skipped four," she said. "That is why it is empty."

Miss Penny nodded. "The number words go in order. Four comes before five." Josephine filled the empty cup last. Then she counted all ten cups with her finger, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Every cup was full.

Max was not grumpy anymore. He took a big sip of juice. "Ten cups, ten sips," he said. Miss Penny gave Josephine a hug. "You counted them all," she said. Josephine sat down with her own cup. Outside the window, a bird flew by. Josephine whispered, "One bird, going home to her nest."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Milan went to the store with Dad. He wanted a book about trucks. He found a blue book on a low shelf. The cover had little marks on it. "Those marks are words," said Dad. "They say truck." Milan traced the marks with his finger. The words told him what the book was.

He opened the book at the front. He turned the pages one by one. The story went from the front to the back. The last page had a big picture of a red truck.

Then the book made a slip of paper fall out. Milan picked it up. It had more words on it. He asked Dad to fetch the shop lady. She read the slip. "This book is from the library," she said. "Someone left it here." Milan held the blue book tight. He wanted to keep it forever. The lady smiled. "You can take it to the library and borrow it," she said. "You can take it home. Then you bring it back, so other kids can read it too." Milan gave the book one more hug. Then he put it in his little bag. "I will bring it back," he said. "But not today."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Ava held her pink backpack tight. It was her first day of school. Mom held her hand. "Where do I put my bag?" Ava asked. "Let's look for your name," said Mom.

There were little boxes on the wall. Ava saw the letter A. Then she saw her whole name, AVA. "That box has my name on it!" she said. She put her pink backpack inside. "My name shows me my spot," said Ava. Mom smiled and nodded.

At snack time, Ava opened her backpack. There was bread from home, and a small surprise too. A sticker was inside, shaped like a star. Ava showed it to her teacher. "You can wear it," said the teacher. Ava stuck it on her shirt. She sat with Mom and ate her bread. "I like my box," said Ava. "It waits for me all day."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Beatrice sat on Grandma's soft couch. She wanted to draw on the tablet. But the screen was dark.

She pushed the little button once. Nothing happened. She pushed it again. Nothing. Then Grandma held her hand over the button. They counted together. "One, two, three." The screen lit up! "It came on because we held it down," said Beatrice.

She found the drawing app. It had a little ball of colors on it. She tapped it and drew a big red ball. "Look, Grandma! A ball!"

When she was done, she tapped the button again. The screen went dark. She helped Grandma sweep the crumbs off the couch. "Tablet sleeps now," said Beatrice.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lucy ran into the playroom. Her big teddy sat on the wide mat. Her small mouse sat in the toy car.

"Teddy wants soup!" said Lucy. She got her little pot. She poured and poured. Oh no! The soup did spill. It went all over the mat.

Lucy looked at the puddle. "Why did it spill?" she asked. She looked at the pot. The pot was small. Teddy was big. A big teddy needs a big pot!

Lucy found the big pot. She poured the soup in. "Drink, Teddy!" she said. Teddy got lots of soup. Not one drop did spill.

Then Lucy pushed the car. She pushed it fast. Then she pushed it slow. Her friend Mouse went for a ride. "Fast!" laughed Lucy. "Slow!" she said next. The car rolled to Teddy's feet.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Adam ran to the red truck at the playground. It was his favorite toy. But Leo was already holding it. Leo pushed the truck on the ground. Vroom, vroom.

Adam grabbed the truck. Leo pulled it back. The truck fell. Both boys made a sad face. The playground felt noisy around them. Miss Maya came over.

"Adam, you can ask for a turn," she said. Adam took a big breath. "Leo, can I have a turn, please?" Leo looked at the truck. He did not let go yet.

"First I go down the slide," Leo said. "Then you can have it." Adam waited on the bench. He counted the slides. One, two, three. Leo ran back with the truck. "Here you go," Leo said. Adam held it tight. "Thank you, Leo," he said. Then Adam drove the truck to Leo. "Your turn now," Adam said. Leo smiled a big smile. "You waited for me," Leo said. "That was kind." Adam clapped his hands. The two boys sat in the sand. They pushed the truck back and forth. Vroom, vroom, all morning long.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Evan sat on the grass with his paints. He had red, blue and yellow. His friend Mia came over with her toy truck. "Can you paint my truck?" she asked. "It can be green like the grass."

Evan looked for green paint. There was no green cup. Evan felt worried. Then he looked at his brush. Yellow paint was on it. He dipped it in the blue cup. He stirred it round and round.

The paint turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," said Evan. He painted the truck green, top to bottom. Mia smiled big. "Thank you," she said. "That was so polite," said Evan's mom from the door. The truck rolled over the green, green grass.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Colton had a library book about bears. He held it at bedtime. The cover felt smooth. He did not want to give it back. He wanted to keep it forever.

"Read it again," Colton said. Dad opened the book. He turned the pages from the front. He went page by page, all the way to the back. The words told Dad what to say. Dad pointed at the words. "These little marks talk," Dad said. Colton looked closely. The marks sat in neat lines. When Dad read them, out came a story about a big brown bear.

The next morning, Colton put the book in his bag. "Where is bear going?" he asked. "Back to the library," said Mom. "Someone else wants to read him too." Colton held the bag tight. His tummy felt funny. He walked slow. He looked at the book one more time.

At the library, Colton set the book on the desk. Then he looked at the shelf. There were lots of books there. He could take a new one home. He picked a book about a red fire truck. The pages felt smooth too. Colton hugged it. "This one talks too," he said. "Read it in the truck?" Dad laughed. "At bedtime," he said. Colton held the book all the way home. "Turn the pages slow," he said. "I want to see every fire truck."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. Tonight was the lantern festival. Everyone would float little boats on the water.

"Can I bring my boat?" Sarah asked. It was a paper boat, soft at the edges. Mama smiled and said yes.

Sarah put a candle in her boat. Then she put in a stone, a flower, and a button. The boat went into the water. It went down, down, down. It sank!

"Why did my boat sink?" Sarah wondered. She looked at Papa's boat. It had only one candle in it. It floated so well.

Sarah counted on her fingers. One candle, one stone, one flower, one button. "Too many things!" she said. "My boat sank because it was too heavy."

She made a new boat. She put in one candle only. Into the water it went. It floated and floated, all the way to the middle of the pool.

The little flame bobbed up and down. Sarah clapped her hands. "Look, Mama! One candle, and it floats!"

Then the flame went pop and turned green for a second. Sarah gasped. "The candle can change colors too?"

Mama laughed and held her hand. "Make a wish, Sarah."

Sarah squeezed her eyes shut. "I wish my boat could float forever."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Kinsley sat on the playroom floor. She had red, blue and yellow paint. She wanted to paint a tree. But she had no green paint. A tree needs green leaves. She looked and looked in the box. No green anywhere.

She made a sound with her mouth. "Hmmm." Then she had an idea. She put some blue paint on her paper. She put some yellow paint on top. She mixed them with her brush. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said. She painted a big tree with high branches. The leaves were all green.

Then she tried more. Red and yellow made orange. Blue and red made purple. Her paper had many colors now. Her big brother came in. "Wow," he said. "How did you get green?" Kinsley held up her brush. "I mixed blue and yellow," she said. "I made it myself."

Her hands were messy. Mom helped her wash them at the sink. The water turned colors as it ran. Then Kinsley ran back to her tree. She painted one more green leaf on the high branch.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Norah came home with a small fish. It was red and shiny. She set the bowl on the table. Her teddy bear sat close by. "The fish will watch us," said Mom.

Norah tapped the bowl. Tap, tap. The fish hid in the little castle. It would not come out. Norah tapped again. The fish hid more. "The fish is hiding because I tap," said Norah. So she stopped tapping. She sat very still. She poured tiny food bits into the water. The bits smelled like the sea.

Then out came the fish. It swam in a circle. It ate the food. It blew a small bubble. Pop! Norah laughed. "Smart fish," she said. Mom hugged her. The teddy bear watched too. The fish swam and swam, happy in its new home.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Weston ran to the playground. He felt excited. His tummy jumped like a bunny.

He saw the tall slide. He wanted to go on it. He climbed up, up, up. Then he looked down. The slide was very tall. His tummy felt cold. His eyes got big. "Mama," he said, "I feel scared."

Mama stood close by. "You can hold my hand," she said. "Scared can get small when Mama is near."

Weston held her hand. He looked down again. The slide did not seem so tall now. His cold tummy turned warm. "Mama is near," he thought. "So scared got small."

He slid down fast. Whee! He laughed. He felt happy. A little girl slid down too. She fell on her bottom. She began to cry. She felt sad.

Weston picked up her hat. It had flown off. "Here," he said. She stopped crying. "Thank you," she said. She smiled a big smile.

Weston felt happy again too. Then a boy grabbed the swing and pushed hard. The little girl frowned. "That makes me mad," she said.

"Tell him with words," said Mama. "Say, I was using that."

The girl said it. The boy said, "Oh, sorry." He got off the swing.

Weston sat on the swing. Mama pushed him. He went high, high, high. A puppy ran up with the boy's ball in its mouth. That was a surprise!

"Big feelings get small," Weston told Mama. "When you say them out." Mama kissed his head. "Yes," she said. "And swings make them small too." Weston laughed all the way down.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to paint her cat. Her cat at home was brown, with round eyes.

She picked up the brown paint. The teacher held up a beet. "This is a root," she said. "It gives us pink paint." Juliette sniffed it. It smelled like dirt.

First Juliette painted a square body. She painted a rectangle tail. Then she painted triangle ears, sharp at the top. Last she cut two little wheels from paper for a cat cart. She cut the wheels square, with four sides.

She pushed the cart. The square wheels would not roll. The corners bumped and stopped.

Juliette waited. She looked at the wheels. Then she cut two new wheels, round like her cat's eyes. Round had no corners. She pushed the cart again. It rolled all the way across the table.

"The corners stopped it," said Juliette. "Round wheels go."

She took a bite of her cracker. It was square, but it tasted just fine.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Zoey sat in the big waiting room. She was going to get her first haircut. She held Mama's hand tight. There was a fish tank near her chair. Zoey did not want the fish to see her cry.

"I don't want them to cut my hair," Zoey said. "It will not grow back."

Mama said, "Let's ask the lady with the scissors."

The hair lady smiled. "I will show you something," she said. She held up a piece of Zoey's hair. Snip. She cut one little piece. Then she put it in Zoey's hand.

"Feel it," the hair lady said. "Your hair is still on your head. Only this bit came off."

Zoey touched her head. Her hair was all still there. "The hair stays on me!" she said. "Only the little piece gets cut."

"Good thinking," the hair lady said. "Now we can cut the rest. You will get a fun new look."

Zoey climbed up into the tall chair. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell like soft snow. It tickled her nose and she laughed.

At dinner that night, Zoey still had her new short hair. Her baby brother made a sour face at his peas. Zoey made a sour face too. Then she smiled.

"My hair got cut," she told him. "And it is still on my head."

She patted her head one more time, just to check.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Oliver went to the cultural center with his mom and his grandpa. It was New Year day. There were red lanterns and drums. The room smelled like warm rice.

Everyone wanted to eat the dumplings. But the dumplings were all gone. Oliver saw a long line at a big table. His tummy made a little growl. "The dumplings are gone because so many people came," he said.

Grandpa held his hand. "We can make more," Grandpa said. They went to the kitchen. Oliver helped fold the dumplings. He pressed the edges with his fingers. The dough was soft and cold. A lady gave him a secret job. He hid one coin in one dumpling, wrapped up pretty in a red paper. "The coin brings luck," she whispered.

The new dumplings went into the hot pot. Soon the line had food again. Oliver ate three. He bit something hard. It was the lucky coin! Grandpa laughed and clapped. Oliver held up the shiny coin. "I found the secret one!" he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Violet put on her red boots at daycare. It had snowed last night. "Yesterday there was no snow," said her friend Ben. "Today the snow is here." Violet looked out the window. The yard was all white and cold.

Teacher Mia held up a big pot. "We will pour warm water on the ice today," she said. "Now we pour. Later we can play." Violet held her little cup. She poured the water on the icy step. The ice went drip, drip, drip.

But Ben poured his water on the snow. The snow stayed white. It did not melt. "Why did my water not work?" Ben asked. Violet looked at her step. Then she looked at his snow. Her water went on hard ice. His water went on soft snow. "The snow is too big," Violet said. "The step is small."

Teacher Mia smiled. "We can try again tomorrow," she said. "Tomorrow the sun will come out. The sun is warm too." Violet clapped her hands.

"Now it is warm water," said Violet. "Later the sun will help." The class lined up at the door. Violet poured one more cup on the step. It went drip, drip, drip again. "Goodbye, ice," said Violet. "See you tomorrow."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Aubrey stood on her helper stool. "Can I do it myself?" she asked. Mom slid the toast to her. The first piece was warm and soft. Aubrey pushed the butter hard. The toast tore and a hole appeared. She looked at the hole. "The toast was too soft," she said. Mom gave her a new piece that was cool and firm. Aubrey pushed the butter again. This time the butter glided. It spread all over. No hole!

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one hand. The jug was big and heavy. Milk sloshed over the side. A puddle grew on the table. "Why did it spill?" she wondered. She looked at the jug, then at the cup. She put the cup on the table and held the jug with two hands. She poured slow, slow, slow. The milk went up, up, up the side. It stopped just at the top. Not one drop spilled.

Aubrey took a big bite of toast and a sip of milk. "The cup needed to sit still," she said. Mom clapped. "You did it all by yourself." Aubrey smiled. "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Felix stood at the big table in the community kitchen. Today he would make his own snack. First, he tried to spread the butter. The butter was cold from the fridge. It tore his toast into little pieces. One piece, two pieces, three pieces.

Then Felix saw the bowl of soft butter sitting by the warm stove. He took a bit on his knife. The soft butter slid across new toast like a smooth road at the beach. "Soft butter does not tear the toast," Felix said.

Next came the milk. Felix held the cup low on the table. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. The cook smiled. "I did it," said Felix. He drank his milk and ate his warm, buttery toast. His itchy sweater sleeve brushed his chin as he grinned.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Evan wanted to paint a green egg at daycare. He looked for green paint. There was no green pot on the table. Only red, blue and yellow were there.

Evan tried red. His egg turned red. "Not green," he said. Miss Kim came over. "Try mixing two colors," she said. Evan dipped his brush in blue. Then he dipped it in yellow. He stirred on the egg. The paint turned green! "It worked!" said Evan. "Blue and yellow make green!"

Tommy hurried over to look. "That is neat!" he said. "Can I try?" Evan gave him the brush. Tommy mixed red and yellow. His egg turned orange. "Wow," said Tommy. "Red and yellow make orange!" Evan smiled and painted a big green stripe. "Mixing is fun," he said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ruby came to Grandma's house. Papa Joe had drive his old blue car to pick her up. Now it was lunch time.

Everyone sat at the big table. Ruby grabbed her spoon. But the spoons did not move. "Why?" she asked. Grandma held out her hands. "We hold hands first," said Grandma. "Then we say thank you."

Papa Joe held one hand. Grandma held the other. Ruby's sock feet did not touch the floor. "Thank you for our food," said Grandma. "Thank you for our food," said Papa Joe. Ruby squeezed her eyes shut. Her voice was small. "Thank you, food!"

Then all the spoons moved at once. "Hey!" said Ruby. "We say it, then we eat!" Grandma laughed. "Yes, smart girl."

After lunch, Ruby had a nap on the fuzzy yellow blanket. She woke up and asked, "Is it dinner yet? I want to say the thank you part."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Mason stood by the curb. The big yellow bus came up the road. It stopped right in front of him. The doors were shut. Mason waited.

The driver pushed a handle. The doors swung open. "The door opens because the driver turns it," Mason said. He held the shiny rail and climbed one step at a time. His hand was small on the big rail.

He found a seat by a window. He looked out at the glass. His mom waved on the sidewalk. Mason waved back. The doors closed with a soft sound, and the bus began to roll. The houses went by the window, one, two, three.

A girl sat down next to him. She had a red backpack, just like Mason. "First day," she said. "First day," said Mason. He felt happy inside.

The bus stopped at the school. The doors opened again, because the driver turned them. Mason held the rail and stepped down. He held his new backpack with both hands. "Bye, bus," he called. The driver smiled and gave a little wave.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Amelia wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked at the paint pots. There was red, yellow, and blue. "No orange," she said. "Where is orange?"

Her friend Tom giggled. "The paint fairy ate it," he said. Amelia laughed. "Silly Tom." She picked up her brush. She put red on her paper. Then she put yellow next to it. She poked the two spots together. The paint squished under her brush. It turned orange!

"Look, look!" said Amelia. She held up her paper. "Red and yellow make orange." She painted a big orange pumpkin. Tom painted a blue nose on his face. It was very silly. Amelia grinned. Orange was her new favorite color. She said, "Red and yellow, sit in the pot!" And they made orange for her work.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Ryan sat at a little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name. He held his pencil in his whole fist. The letters came out wobbly. The Y looked like a squiggle.

The librarian, Miss Kim, sat down next to him. She did not say much. She just pinched her own pencil with two fingers. Ryan watched. He thought about the crab at the beach. The crab pinches with two claws.

Ryan pinched the pencil with two fingers too. Now his hand felt steady. He wrote a big R. It came out clear. He wrote the Y. Then A. Then N.

"Look," Ryan said. "The letters come out right because I pinch!"

Miss Kim smiled. "Yes, they do." Ryan frowned at the paper. "My juice made my mouth sour. Writing did not."

He wrote his name one more time. The last N was the best one.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Grayson looked out the window. Big white flakes fell down. No school today! He ran to tell Mom. "Mom, wake up! Snow!"

Mom smiled. "The snow came in the night. The roads are all white, so no cars can drive. That is why school is closed." Grayson clapped his hands. "A snow day!"

He wanted to build a snowman. But first he needed his boots. He could not find one boot anywhere. "Mom, help! My boot is lost!"

Mom got down on the floor. She looked under the bed. There it was, under Grayson's toy plane. "Your boot was hiding," said Mom.

Grayson pulled on his boots. The snow was deep and bumpy. He made a big round snowman with Dad. Then he gave Mom a carrot for the nose. "Snow closed school," said Grayson, "so we can play all day."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Felix stood by the wooden fence. It was his first day of school. He wanted a friend to play with. But all the kids were new too. Nobody knew his name. He tried to say hello. The kids ran to the slide. Nobody knew his name.

Then Felix looked down. His teacher had pinned a picture card on his shirt. It was a tag with his name on it. A girl pointed at it. "Felix!" she read. "Do you want to play tag?" Felix smiled big. "Yes!" he said.

Felix ran and ran. When he got tired, he looked at his tag. He remembered why the girl knew his name. "The tag told her," he said. The girl laughed. "I have a tag too! It says Mia." They held hands by the fence.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Isabella went to Ms. Rosa's music room. She saw a shiny drum and a little toy cat. The cat had a long tail.

"I want to sing the whole song," said Isabella.

"First we find the beat," said Ms. Rosa. She tapped the drum. One, two. One, two.

Isabella clapped too. But she clapped fast, fast, fast! She got to the end of "Twinkle, twinkle" before the drum did. "Oops," she said. "I ran away from my song!"

Ms. Rosa laughed. "Clap when the drum claps. One, two. One, two."

Isabella looked at the drum. She waited. Drum, clap. Drum, clap. Then she sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The song stayed with the drum the whole way.

"I did it!" said Isabella. "The drum holds my song."

"Then the cat wants a turn," said Ms. Rosa. The cat tapped the beat with its tail. One, two. One, two.

Isabella clapped and sang. The cat's tail went up, up, up.

"Next time, can the cat sing too?" asked Isabella.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Zachary stood in the school computer lab. He wanted to draw a big blue pond on the tablet. But the screen was dark. "It is broken," he said.

Miss Ana smiled. "Just press the round button," she said. "Hold it down and count." Zachary pressed the little round button. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen lit up like morning. "The button makes it turn on!" he said.

He tapped the green drawing app. It opened with a pop sound. He drew a blue pond with three fish. Then it was time for lunch. Miss Ana said, "Push the button to make it sleep." Zachary held the button again. The screen went dark. He set the tablet on the shelf, careful and slow.

"Look, Miss Ana," he said. "I pressed it, and it went to sleep."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Elizabeth's grandma came to stay. She would sleep in the guest room for seven whole days. Elizabeth counted them on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said.

The guest bed had big soft blankets. Grandma tucked them in tight, like a nest. But at night, Grandma could not sleep. Elizabeth heard her turn and turn. In the morning, Grandma had dark circles under her eyes.

Elizabeth thought and thought. The room faced the street. Cars went by with bright lights. "The light wakes Grandma up," Elizabeth said. So she found a thick quilt and hung it over the window. That night, the room stayed dark and still.

Grandma slept and slept. In the morning she smiled. "What a good sleep," she said. "I love this cozy room." Elizabeth loved it too. She counted the days left. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Stay in your nest, Grandma."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jasmine went to the park with her dad. They wanted a picnic in the sun. The sky was sunny and bright. "Yay, sun!" said Jasmine. She wore her shiny red hat. It was shiny because the sun made it glow.

Then the wind began to blow. The wind blew her hat right off. It blew the leaves. It blew the trees. "Why did the sun go away?" Jasmine asked. She looked up. "The wind moved a big gray cloud," she said. "The cloud took the sun away." Then rain began to fall. Drip, drop, drip.

"Rain needs rain boots," said Dad. He helped Jasmine put on her yellow coat. She pulled the hood up over her neck. "The hood keeps the rain off my neck," she said. They sat under the roof by the swings. They ate crackers and watched the rain. "Rainy days are good too," said Jasmine. She put out her hand and caught a drop.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Mohamed sat in his big bed. He had a library book about a turtle. "Turtle," he said, pointing at the picture. He turned the page. More turtle! He turned another page. The pages went from the front to the back.

On the last page there were little black marks. "What are those?" Mohamed asked. His dad read them out loud. They said the turtle could grow big in the pond. The marks were words! Words told about the turtle. Mohamed looked and looked. Did the book have more words? He turned the book around. The room went dizzy for a second. The book was all upside down.

"I want to keep this book forever," Mohamed said. He hugged it tight. Dad shook his head. "It has to go back to the library tomorrow. It is library day." Mohamed felt sad. "Why does it go back?" he asked. Dad said other kids want to read it too. Mohamed thought and thought. Other kids. Reading his turtle book?

"Can we get it again?" Mohamed asked. "Yes," said Dad. Mohamed put the book by his shoes so he would not forget it. In the morning, the book waited by the door. Mohamed patted the cover. "Bye, turtle book," he said. "A new kid will read you now."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Samuel went out to the backyard in the morning. The sun was shining. It was sunny. But Samuel wanted to build in his sandpit, and he could not see. The sun was too bright in his eyes.

"What can help me?" he asked. He ran inside and got his hat. He put the big hat on his head. Now the sun was out of his eyes. Samuel could build his sand castle. "The hat helps because it stops the sun," he said.

Then the wind came. It was windy. The wind blew his hat away! "Oh no," said Samuel. The wind blew and blew. He held his hat with one hand and patted the sand with the other. The wind stopped, and the yard was quiet again. Samuel smiled and put the last scoop on his castle.
